text:
This paper solves the problem of how to classify text quickly and efficiently [P2_p1_c02]. Traditional linear classifiers can struggle to generalize when there are many possible categories and few examples [P2_p1_c04]. 

The main idea is a text classifier called fastText [P2_p1_c02]. It represents sentences by grouping words together and adds local word order information using n-grams, which are sequences of words [P2_p1_c04][P2_p2_c03]. 

Regarding cost and speed, the paper shows that fastText is many orders of magnitude faster for training and evaluation than deep learning classifiers [P2_p1_c02]. It can be trained on more than one billion words in less than ten minutes using a standard multi-core computer processor [P2_p1_c02]. It can also classify half a million sentences across 312K categories in less than a minute [P2_p1_c02]. 

In terms of accuracy, fastText is often on par with deep learning classifiers [P2_p1_c02]. For sentiment analysis, its accuracy is slightly better than some existing methods like char-CNN and char-CRNN, though a bit worse than VDCNN [P2_p3_c02]. Adding word pairs called bigrams improves performance by 1% to 4% [P2_p3_c02]. 

As for limitations, fastText does not use pre-trained word embeddings, which can explain a 1% difference in accuracy compared to certain other approaches [P2_p3_c02]. The sources do not mention any other limitations.
